why_how.text: Every registered car in Florida must carry two coverages, and letting them lapse can cost you your license.

scenario.text: Morgan plans to cancel car insurance after selling the car but still has the plates.

reasoning.text: Plates must go back before the policy cancels, or a lapse can suspend the license.

result.text: Morgan surrenders the plates first and then cancels the policy.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking injury coverage pays for damage you cause to another person's property.

correction.text: Injury coverage pays your own hurt regardless of fault, while property coverage pays damage you cause others.

memory_support.text: Injury pays you, property pays them.

prompt.text: Which coverage pays for your own injuries no matter who caused the crash?

rationale.text: Injury benefits pay your own hurt regardless of fault.

lines.text: Two required coverages
Lapses and their penalties
Higher responsibility tiers

narration.text: Driving in Florida starts with insurance, and this lesson explains what you must carry and what happens if you do not. Before a car can be registered, it needs two coverages: injury coverage and property coverage. Each has a minimum amount, it must stay continuous, and proof must ride in the car. If coverage lapses, insurers report it to the state and the license can be suspended. Finally, some drivers must prove a higher level of financial responsibility after a crash, a DUI or other serious cases. Let us take these pieces one at a time.

lines.text: Injury benefits pay your own hurt, regardless of fault
Property benefits pay damage you cause others
At least ten thousand dollars of each

narration.text: Registration needs injury and property coverage in place first. Injury benefits pay for your own injuries no matter who was at fault. Property benefits pay for damage you cause to other people's property. You must carry at least ten thousand dollars of each kind, bought from a carrier licensed in Florida. You prove the coverage when you register, keep it continuous, and keep proof in the car. A simple way to hold the pair is that injury coverage pays you, and property coverage pays the people whose property you damage.

lines.text: Cars here ninety of the last three hundred sixty-five days stay insured
Carriers report lapses
Plates go back before a policy cancels

narration.text: A car that has been in Florida for ninety days of the last three hundred sixty-five must stay insured. Insurance carriers report lapses to the state, and failing to keep coverage can suspend a license for up to three years. In a worked example, Morgan sells a car and wants to cancel the insurance but still holds the plates. The rule is that plates go back before the policy cancels. So Morgan surrenders the plates first and then cancels, which avoids a lapse suspension. Cancelling first and returning plates later is the order that causes trouble.

lines.text: No proof at a stop: prove coverage in court
Reinstatement after a lapse conviction: one hundred fifty to five hundred dollars
Long suspensions bring more penalties

narration.text: If an officer stops you and you have no proof of insurance, you must prove coverage in court or face suspension. Reinstating after a convicted lapse costs between one hundred fifty and five hundred dollars. A forged insurance card is far more serious than a missing one: missing proof forces a court date, while a forged card forces an arrest, and fake cards are punished as misdemeanors. Once a suspension passes thirty days, plates can be seized, jail of up to a year with a one thousand dollar fine is possible, temporary licenses are barred, and hearings are granted on request.

lines.text: After a crash: insurance or a state certificate
DUI: one hundred, three hundred and fifty thousand dollars for three years
Lesser cases: ten, twenty and ten thousand, or thirty combined

narration.text: Drivers in a crash prove financial responsibility with insurance or a state certificate. Some drivers must carry more. A driver convicted of DUI carries tiers of one hundred thousand, three hundred thousand and fifty thousand dollars for three years. Point, crash, habitual-offender and serious-offense cases carry tiers of ten thousand, twenty thousand and ten thousand dollars, or thirty thousand dollars combined. In those cases a lapse can suspend for up to three years, and at-fault damages must be paid first. The DUI tiers are much higher than the tiers for the lesser triggers.

title.text: Injury coverage is not property coverage

lines.text: Injury: your own hurt
Property: damage you cause others

narration.text: A frequent mix-up is thinking the injury coverage pays for anything that goes wrong in a crash. It does not. Injury coverage pays your own injuries regardless of fault. Damage you cause to another person's property is paid by property coverage. Another trap is the order of steps when cancelling insurance: the plates go back first, before the policy cancels, or the lapse can lead to a suspension. Keep both coverages at the ten thousand dollar minimum, keep them continuous, and keep proof in the car at all times. Two coverages, two jobs, and the plates go back first.

lines.text: Your own injuries in a crash
Which coverage pays?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: after a crash, which coverage pays for your own injuries, no matter who caused the crash? Commit to your answer first. The answer is personal injury coverage. Injury benefits pay your own hurt regardless of fault, while property benefits pay damage you cause to others. Both coverages are required before registration, each at a minimum of ten thousand dollars from a Florida-licensed carrier, kept continuous, with proof kept in the car. If the question instead asked about damage to another driver's car, the answer would be property coverage.

lines.text: Two coverages, ten thousand each
Plates back before cancelling

narration.text: To recap, registration needs injury and property coverage, at least ten thousand dollars of each, from a Florida-licensed carrier, kept continuous with proof in the car. Cars here ninety of the last three hundred sixty-five days stay insured, carriers report lapses, and lapses can suspend for up to three years unless plates go back first. Missing proof means proving coverage in court, a forged card means arrest, and DUI convicts carry the highest responsibility tiers for three years, far above the tiers for lesser triggers.

why_how.text: Teen driving hours change with age, and misusing a license or a disabled permit is a crime.

scenario.text: Taylor is sixteen and wants to drive home from a party at midnight.

reasoning.text: Sixteen-year-olds may not drive from eleven at night to six in the morning unless driving for work or with a companion aged twenty-one or older.

result.text: Taylor needs a companion aged twenty-one or older, or must not drive home at midnight.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking sixteen- and seventeen-year-olds share the same curfew.

correction.text: Sixteen-year-olds stop from eleven at night to six in the morning, while seventeen-year-olds stop from one to five in the morning.

memory_support.text: Sixteen: eleven to six. Seventeen: one to five.

prompt.text: A seventeen-year-old wants to drive alone at two in the morning, not for work. Is it allowed?

answer.text: No, seventeen-year-olds may not drive from one to five in the morning without an exception.

rationale.text: The exceptions are driving for work or with a companion aged twenty-one or older.

lines.text: Teen driving hours
License crimes
Disabled parking permits

narration.text: This lesson covers three topics that are short but full of details. First are the hours when young drivers may be on the road, which change from the learner stage to sixteen and seventeen. Second is the list of crimes involving licenses, from lending a license to giving false statements. Third are disabled parking permits, what they allow, and what happens when someone uses a permit that belongs to another person. Pay attention to the exact hours and penalties, because questions often change one number to test you.

lines.text: Learners: daylight only for three months, then until ten at night
Sixteen: no driving eleven at night to six in the morning
Seventeen: no driving one to five in the morning

narration.text: A learner minor may drive only in daylight until three months have passed, and after that until ten at night. Sixteen-year-olds may not drive from eleven at night to six in the morning. Seventeen-year-olds may not drive from one in the morning to five in the morning. All of these limits are excused when the teen is driving to or from work or has a companion aged twenty-one or older. In a worked example, Taylor is sixteen and wants to drive home at midnight. Without a work reason or a companion aged twenty-one or older, Taylor may not make that drive.

lines.text: Altering, misusing or lending a license
Fraudulent applications and dual credentials
False statements to officers, courts or crash reports

narration.text: Florida treats several license acts as crimes. Altering a license, misusing one or lending it to someone else are all crimes. So are fraudulent applications and holding two credentials at once. Lending or renting a vehicle to an unlicensed driver is on the list too. Finally, giving false statements to officers, to courts or on crash reports is a license crime. The common thread is honesty and control: your license is yours alone, it must not be altered or shared, and what you tell officials about it must be true. Each of these acts is listed as a crime involving licenses.

lines.text: Waive meter fees, open reserved spaces while transporting the owner
Borrowed permit: misdemeanor, five hundred dollars or six months
Towing and confiscation

narration.text: A disabled parking permit waives meter fees and opens reserved spaces while the vehicle is transporting the permit owner. Using a borrowed permit is a misdemeanor, punishable by a fine of five hundred dollars or six months, and it brings towing and confiscation of the permit. So a proper permit grants real privileges, but only when it is used by or for its owner. A family member who parks in a reserved space with the owner's permit while the owner is not in the car is not using the permit properly. The privileges belong to the trips that carry the owner.

lines.text: Sixteen: eleven at night to six in the morning
Seventeen: one to five in the morning

narration.text: The trap here is treating the sixteen and seventeen curfews as one rule. They are different. At sixteen the no-driving window runs from eleven at night to six in the morning. At seventeen it shrinks to one in the morning to five in the morning. Both share the same exceptions: driving for work, or with a companion aged twenty-one or older. And learners have their own earlier rule, daylight only for the first three months and then until ten at night. Match the age to the window before you answer. Learners, sixteen-year-olds and seventeen-year-olds each have their own rule.

lines.text: Seventeen, alone, two in the morning
Allowed or not?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a seventeen-year-old wants to drive alone at two in the morning, and the trip is not for work. Is that allowed? Make your choice before continuing. The answer is no. Seventeen-year-olds may not drive from one in the morning to five in the morning. The only exceptions are driving for work or having a companion aged twenty-one or older, and neither applies here. A sixteen-year-old would face an even longer window, from eleven at night to six in the morning. Working or riding with a companion aged twenty-one or older would change the answer.

lines.text: Learners, sixteen and seventeen each differ
Borrowed permits are a misdemeanor

narration.text: To recap, learner minors drive in daylight only for three months and then until ten at night. Sixteen-year-olds may not drive from eleven at night to six in the morning, and seventeen-year-olds from one to five in the morning, with exceptions for work or a companion aged twenty-one or older. Altering, misusing or lending a license, fraudulent applications, dual credentials and false statements are crimes. Disabled permits waive meters and open reserved spaces for the owner, while borrowed permits bring a misdemeanor, towing and confiscation.

why_how.text: DUI penalties rise sharply with each conviction, and refusing a test carries its own suspension.

scenario.text: Casey is arrested for DUI and refuses the breath test for the first time.

reasoning.text: A first refusal brings an automatic one-year suspension, and drivers have consented to testing by implied consent.

result.text: Casey's license is suspended for one year because of the refusal.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking that refusing a chemical test avoids a suspension.

correction.text: A first refusal suspends one year automatically, and a second brings eighteen months plus a misdemeanor.

prompt.text: A driver refuses a chemical test for the second time. What follows?

answer.text: Eighteen months of suspension and a misdemeanor.

rationale.text: A first refusal costs one year, while a second costs eighteen months plus a misdemeanor.

lines.text: What DUI covers
Refusal penalties
First to third convictions

narration.text: This lesson covers driving under the influence: what it includes, how testing works, what refusing a test costs, and how penalties rise from a first to a third conviction. We will also look at the stricter rules for drivers under twenty-one and what can happen to a car used in a drug felony. DUI penalties have many parts, including fines, jail, revoked days, school hours, an addiction check and an ignition interlock. The pattern to remember is that nearly every part grows with each new conviction. Each part of the penalty list is worth learning on its own.

lines.text: First refusal: one year, automatic
Second refusal: eighteen months and a misdemeanor
Fatal or injury crashes: professional blood draw

narration.text: Refusing a chemical test does not avoid trouble. A first refusal suspends the license for one year automatically. A second refusal stretches the suspension to eighteen months and adds a misdemeanor charge. When a crash causes death or injury, a professional blood draw is required even if the driver is unconscious. In a worked example, Casey is arrested for DUI and refuses the breath test for the first time. Because drivers have already consented to testing, the refusal itself brings a one-year suspension for Casey.

lines.text: Five hundred to one thousand dollars, fifty service hours
A year of probation, six months jail, one hundred eighty revoked days
Twelve school hours, addiction check, possible interlock

narration.text: A first DUI conviction draws a fine of five hundred to one thousand dollars, fifty hours of community service and a year of probation. The penalty list also includes six months of jail, one hundred eighty days of revocation, twelve hours of school, an addiction check, and a possible ignition interlock. All of these become harsher when the blood alcohol level is high or a young passenger was in the car. Notice that even a first conviction carries a long list of penalties, not just a fine, and that the school requirement for a first conviction is twelve hours.

lines.text: Second: one to two thousand dollars, nine months, one year interlock
Third: two to five thousand dollars, twelve months, two interlock years
Both: one hundred eighty revoked days, twenty-one school hours

narration.text: A second DUI draws one thousand to two thousand dollars, nine months of jail, one hundred eighty revoked days, twenty-one school hours, an addiction check and a year of ignition interlock, with fines doubled when the case is enhanced. A third DUI draws two thousand to five thousand dollars, twelve months of jail, one hundred eighty revoked days, twenty-one school hours, an addiction check and two years of interlock. Fines, jail, schooling and interlock all climb across first, second and third convictions, while the revoked days stay at one hundred eighty in each list.

lines.text: Point zero two: six months lost
Point zero five: substance course; parent notice under nineteen
Any drug conviction: license lost

narration.text: Drivers under twenty-one face much lower limits. At a blood alcohol level of point zero two they lose the license for six months. At point zero five they must also take a substance course, and for drivers under nineteen, parents are notified. Any drug conviction costs a driver under twenty-one the license. Separately, a car used to haul or sell drugs, or to help a drug felony, may be seized and forfeited as contraband. These rules show how tightly Florida links young drivers and drugs to the driving privilege. These limits sit far below the point zero eight arrest level.

lines.text: First refusal: one year
Second refusal: eighteen months plus a misdemeanor

narration.text: Some drivers believe that refusing a chemical test avoids the consequences of a DUI arrest. The handbook says the opposite. Holding a license means implied consent to testing, and a first refusal suspends the license for one year automatically. A second refusal brings eighteen months and a misdemeanor. In crashes that cause death or injury, a professional blood draw happens even if the driver is unconscious. So refusing adds its own penalty on top of whatever the DUI case brings, rather than replacing it. Refusal is never a way out of testing.

lines.text: A second chemical test refusal
What follows?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a driver refuses a chemical test for the second time. What follows? Decide before going on. The answer is an eighteen-month suspension and a misdemeanor charge. A first refusal costs one year automatically, and the second stretches that to eighteen months while adding the misdemeanor. Testing rests on implied consent, which means the license itself carries the agreement to be tested for alcohol or drugs when a driver is arrested for DUI. The first refusal is one year, so the second refusal is the one that adds the misdemeanor and stretches to eighteen months.

lines.text: Any impairing substance counts
Penalties climb with each conviction

narration.text: To recap, DUI covers alcohol and controlled, prescription or store-bought drugs, a license is suspended at arrest at point zero eight or on refusal, and implied consent compels testing. A first refusal costs one year, a second eighteen months plus a misdemeanor. Fines, jail, school hours and interlock climb from a first to a third conviction, with one hundred eighty revoked days in each. Drivers under twenty-one lose six months at point zero two, and cars used in drug felonies may be forfeited as contraband. Each new conviction raises the stakes.

why_how.text: School bus and restraint rules protect children, and breaking them carries points, fines and more.

scenario.text: Drew is driving with a four-year-old and a nine-year-old passenger.

reasoning.text: Ages four and five ride seated with a belt or boosted, under-thirteen riders belong in back, and the driver answers for minors.

result.text: Drew seats both children in back, belts or boosts the four-year-old, and is responsible for both.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking an airbag can take the place of a seat belt.

correction.text: Belts must cross the hips and chest, and airbags never substitute for them.

memory_support.text: Hips and chest, kids in back.

prompt.text: Who is responsible for making sure a fifteen-year-old passenger is belted?

rationale.text: Drivers answer for minors, while adults answer for themselves.

lines.text: Roadway litter penalties
School bus passing
Belts and child seats

narration.text: This lesson brings together three rules about care for the road and the people around you. First is litter: small amounts and heavy dumps carry very different penalties. Second is passing a school bus illegally, which brings points and fines, and much more if someone is hurt. Third are seat belts and child restraints: how belts must be worn, where young children ride, which ages need car seats or boosters, who is responsible for each rider, and which people are exempt. Expect specific ages and amounts throughout. Each rule comes with its own numbers.

lines.text: Litter to fifteen pounds: one hundred dollars
Heavier: misdemeanor, one thousand dollars, three points, cleanup
Bus passing: citation, school, four points, a fine

narration.text: Roadway litter up to fifteen pounds costs one hundred dollars. Heavier dumps bring a misdemeanor charge, a one thousand dollar fine, three points and cleanup duty. Passing a school bus illegally draws a citation, a required course, four points and a fine of two hundred sixty-five or four hundred sixty-five dollars. If the passing injures someone, the driver also faces one hundred twenty service hours, a panel, six points, a year without driving and a fine of fifteen hundred dollars. So injury changes a bus passing case dramatically.

lines.text: Across the hips and chest
Never behind the back
Airbags never substitute

narration.text: Belts must cross the hips and chest. Tucking the shoulder belt behind your back is not allowed, and an airbag never takes the place of a belt. Child seats must fit the child, the car and the caregiver, and riders under thirteen belong in the back seat. The handbook also notes that driving on wheel rims damages roads and is unlawful. In short, the belt is worn correctly every time, the airbag is only an addition, and the youngest riders sit in back where the handbook places them. A belt worn behind the back does not meet the rule, even with an airbag in front.

lines.text: Belts bind drivers, front riders and passengers under eighteen
Under four: car seats; four and five: seated or boosted
Drivers answer for minors; adults for themselves

narration.text: Rear-facing seats must never face an airbag. In a hired ride, providing restraints for a child falls on the parents. Belts are required for drivers, front-seat passengers and passengers under eighteen. Children under four need car seats, and children aged four and five ride seated with a belt or in a booster. Drivers answer for minors, while adults answer for themselves, and free fitting help is available. In a worked example, Drew seats a four-year-old and a nine-year-old in back, belts or boosts the younger child, and is responsible for both.

lines.text: Certified medical cases, paper carriers
Old school buses, paid buses, farm gear
Trucks past twenty-six thousand pounds

narration.text: A short list of riders and vehicles is exempt from the belt rules. It covers people with a certified medical exemption, paper carriers on their routes, older school buses, buses carrying paying passengers, farm equipment, and trucks heavier than twenty-six thousand pounds. There is also an exemption for children aged four and five when riding as a favor or in an emergency. Outside this list, the belt rules apply. Notice that the truck exemption depends on weight, so an ordinary pickup does not qualify. If a rider is not on this list, the belt rules apply to them.

lines.text: Belts across hips and chest
Airbags never substitute

narration.text: The trap is believing an airbag makes the belt optional. It never does. The belt must cross the hips and chest, never behind the back, and the airbag only adds protection. A related trap concerns children. Rear-facing seats must never face an airbag, and riders under thirteen belong in the back seat. When a question describes a front-seat child or a belt tucked behind someone's back, the rule has been broken. Remember also who answers: drivers for minors, adults for themselves. Check where each child sits and how each belt crosses the body.

lines.text: A fifteen-year-old passenger
Who makes sure they are belted?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a fifteen-year-old passenger rides in your car. Who is responsible for making sure that passenger is belted? Settle your answer before continuing. The answer is the driver. Drivers answer for minors, while adult passengers answer for themselves. Belts are required for drivers, front-seat riders and every passenger under eighteen, so a fifteen-year-old must be belted wherever they sit, and the driver is the one who answers for it. An adult passenger, by contrast, answers for their own belt, not the driver.

lines.text: Fifteen pounds is the litter line
Drivers answer for minors

narration.text: To recap, litter up to fifteen pounds costs one hundred dollars, while heavier dumps bring a misdemeanor, one thousand dollars, three points and cleanup. School bus passing brings four points and a fine, and injurious passing adds service hours, six points, a year out and fifteen hundred dollars. Belts cross hips and chest and airbags never substitute. Under-thirteen riders sit in back, under-fours need car seats, fours and fives are seated or boosted, drivers answer for minors, and a short list of exemptions applies.

why_how.text: Points build toward suspension, so knowing what each violation costs helps you protect your license.

scenario.text: Jesse collects twelve points within one year.

reasoning.text: Twelve points in a year suspends the license for thirty days.

result.text: Jesse's license is suspended for thirty days.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking out-of-state convictions do not count toward Florida point suspensions.

correction.text: Out-of-state convictions count equally toward the point totals.

prompt.text: A driver reaches eighteen points within eighteen months. How long is the suspension?

rationale.text: Eighteen points in eighteen months suspends the license for three months.

lines.text: Limits and speeding fines
Crash course rules
Point totals and values

narration.text: This lesson covers how speeding and crashes affect your license. We start with speed limits and the fines for extreme speeding and zone speeding. Then we look at when a crash forces a driver into a course, and what follows a third crash offense. Finally we cover the point system: the totals that suspend a license, the special rule for minors, and how many points different violations carry. The numbers are many, so we will group them by what they measure: fines, crash deadlines, point totals and point values. Keep each group of numbers separate.

lines.text: Know and obey limits; Florida caps them at seventy
More than fifty over: one thousand, then two thousand five hundred dollars
School or work zones double fines toward one thousand dollars

narration.text: Every motorist must know and obey the speed limits, and Florida caps them at seventy miles per hour. Speeding tickets cost fines and points. Going more than fifty miles per hour over the limit costs one thousand dollars, and two thousand five hundred dollars after that. Speeding in a school or work zone doubles the fine, up toward one thousand dollars, and a course may be required. So extreme speeding brings the largest fixed fines, while zone speeding doubles the ordinary fine. Both are on top of the points a speeding ticket adds.

lines.text: Charged drivers face court on officer-filed counts
Injury crash or second collision in two years: avoidance course
Third offense in thirty-six months: retraining within ninety days

narration.text: A driver charged after a crash faces court on the counts the officer files. An at-fault crash with injury, or a second collision within two years, forces a collision-avoidance course. A third crash offense within thirty-six months goes further: a twelve-hour advanced course, four hours behind the wheel and an extended test. If those are not completed within ninety days, the license lapses to cancellation. The steps grow with each crash, from court, to a course, to full retraining with a deadline attached. Missing the ninety-day deadline is what turns retraining into cancellation.

lines.text: Twelve in a year: thirty days
Eighteen in eighteen months: three months
Twenty-four in thirty-six months: one year

narration.text: Point totals lead to suspensions on a fixed scale. Twelve points within one year suspends the license for thirty days. Eighteen points within eighteen months suspends it for three months. Twenty-four points within thirty-six months suspends it for a year. Out-of-state convictions count equally toward these totals. In a worked example, Jesse collects twelve points within one year, so Jesse's license is suspended for thirty days. Each step up needs more points over a longer window and brings a longer suspension. The windows grow as the totals grow.

lines.text: Speeding: three to fifteen over, four past sixteen, six with a crash
Leaving a scene with damage over fifty dollars: six
Signals, bus passing, reckless: four; curfew and handheld zones: three

narration.text: Speeding draws three points up to fifteen over, four points past sixteen over, and six points when it causes a crash. Leaving the scene of a crash with damage over fifty dollars draws six points. Texting draws three points on its own, more in school zones, and six in a crash. Signal violations, school bus passing and reckless driving draw four points each, and passing a school bus with injury draws six. Driving during restricted hours and handheld device use in protected zones draw three points each. Crashes and injuries push the point values higher.

lines.text: Out-of-state convictions count equally
Minors fall at six points

narration.text: Two traps sit in the point rules. First, some drivers think tickets from another state do not count in Florida. They do: out-of-state convictions count equally toward the point totals. Second, drivers sometimes apply the adult twelve-point line to minors. A minor who reaches six points in a year drops to business-only driving for a year, with ninety days added for each further point. So read the age and the place of each ticket in a question before deciding whether a threshold has been reached. Six points for a minor, twelve for the first adult step.

lines.text: Eighteen points in eighteen months
How long is the suspension?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a driver reaches eighteen points within eighteen months. How long is the suspension? Choose your answer before you continue. The answer is three months. The scale runs thirty days at twelve points in a year, three months at eighteen points in eighteen months, and one year at twenty-four points in thirty-six months. Out-of-state convictions count equally toward each of these totals, so a ticket from another state still adds to the count. Twelve points in a year would bring thirty days instead, and twenty-four points in thirty-six months would bring a full year.

lines.text: Seventy is the cap
Twelve, eighteen, twenty-four

narration.text: To recap, Florida caps speed limits at seventy, extreme speeding costs one thousand then two thousand five hundred dollars, and zone speeding doubles fines. Injury crashes or a second collision in two years force a course, and a third crash offense in thirty-six months forces retraining within ninety days. Points suspend at twelve, eighteen and twenty-four over growing windows, minors drop to business-only at six, and point values step from three to four to six depending on the violation and whether a crash or injury occurred.

why_how.text: Knowing the difference between a suspension, a revocation and a cancellation tells you what it takes to drive again.

scenario.text: Avery's license was issued after Avery used false papers.

reasoning.text: A license won by false papers is cancelled, which voids it from the start.

result.text: Avery's license is cancelled rather than suspended or revoked.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking suspension, revocation and cancellation all mean the same thing.

correction.text: Suspension puts privileges on hold, revocation ends them, and cancellation voids them from the start.

prompt.text: A license is found to have been obtained with false papers. Which action applies?

rationale.text: Cancellation voids licenses issued wrongly or won by false papers.

lines.text: Suspension, revocation, cancellation
Review offices and hearings

narration.text: This lesson separates the three ways Florida can take away driving privileges and explains where a driver goes for relief. A suspension puts privileges on hold, a revocation ends them, and a cancellation voids a license as if it had never been properly issued. Each has its own list of grounds. We will finish with the review offices that handle hardship and reinstatement, the ten-day window to appeal certain DUI suspensions, and the option first offenders have to trade review rights for a restricted license. Each action has its own list of grounds.

lines.text: Fraudulent applications, unlawful use, court orders, test refusals
Restricted-license misuse, point totals, unpaid fines, no-shows
Support lapses, missing insurance, bus failures, retail theft, dropouts

narration.text: Suspension starts with fraudulent applications, unlawful use of a license, court orders, and refusals of intoxication tests. It continues through misuse of a restricted license, point totals, unpaid fines and failures to appear, lapses in support payments, missing insurance, school bus violations, retail theft and dropping out of school. The list is long, but the idea is consistent: a suspension puts the privilege on hold while a problem is resolved. Once the reason is cleared, the driver goes through reinstatement rather than starting over.

lines.text: Intoxicated driving, vehicle felonies, deadly hit-and-runs
Ownership lies, triple recklessness, major histories
Drug felonies, failed vision, racing

narration.text: Revocation ends driving privileges. Its grounds include intoxicated driving, felonies involving a vehicle, hit-and-runs causing death, lying about vehicle ownership, three reckless driving convictions, using a vehicle for immoral purposes, major or point-count histories, drug felonies, failed vision and racing. These are among the most serious grounds in the handbook. Where a suspension puts the privilege on hold, a revocation ends it, so the driver is not simply waiting out a period on a license that still exists.

lines.text: Licenses issued wrongly
Licenses won by false papers
Licenses tied to unfinished schooling

narration.text: Cancellation voids a license. It applies to licenses that were issued wrongly, licenses obtained with false papers, and licenses tied to schooling that was never finished. In a worked example, Avery's license was issued after Avery used false papers. That license is cancelled, which means it is void from the start rather than put on hold or ended. Cancellation is about whether the license should have existed at all, which is why it differs from both suspension and revocation. Cancelling the license reflects that it should not have been issued at all.

lines.text: Review offices handle hardship and reinstatement
DUI alcohol and refusal appeals: hearing within ten days of arrest
First offenders may trade review rights for a restricted license

narration.text: Hardship requests and reinstatement run through review offices. For a DUI suspension based on alcohol level or test refusal, an appeal needs a hearing requested within ten days of the arrest. First offenders have another option there: they may give up their review rights in exchange for a restricted license. Ten days is short, so a driver who wants to challenge such a suspension must act quickly. The review office is the place for both the appeal and the restricted license option. Waiting past those ten days would miss the window for that hearing.

lines.text: Suspension holds
Revocation ends
Cancellation voids

narration.text: The trap is using the three words interchangeably. They are not the same. A suspension puts privileges on hold, revocation ends them, and cancellation voids them from the start. Grounds help you tell them apart: unpaid fines or point totals point to suspension, racing or a deadly hit-and-run points to revocation, and false papers or a wrongly issued license point to cancellation. A memory line is hold, end, or void. Match the ground in the question to the word before you choose. The ground in the question is the clue to the right word.

lines.text: A license won by false papers
Which action applies?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a license turns out to have been obtained with false papers. Which action applies, suspension, revocation or cancellation? Decide before going on. The answer is cancellation. Cancellation voids licenses that were issued wrongly, won by false papers, or tied to unfinished schooling. A suspension would only put the privilege on hold, and a revocation would end it, but a license obtained with false papers is treated as void from the start. Unfinished schooling and a wrongly issued license lead to the same result, cancellation.

lines.text: Hold, end, or void
Ten days to seek a hearing

narration.text: To recap, suspension puts privileges on hold for grounds such as fraud, unlawful use, test refusals, point totals, unpaid fines and missing insurance. Revocation ends privileges for grounds such as intoxicated driving, vehicle felonies, deadly hit-and-runs, triple recklessness, drug felonies, failed vision and racing. Cancellation voids licenses issued wrongly, won by false papers or tied to unfinished schooling. Review offices handle hardship and reinstatement, and DUI alcohol and refusal appeals need a hearing within ten days of arrest.
